sections.body:
An **insect** is a small animal with six legs and a body in three parts. That is the whole test. If it has six legs and three body parts, it is an insect.

Insects live everywhere. They walk on the ground, live in water, hide under stones, fly in the air, and even live inside other plants. Ants, bees, butterflies, beetles, flies, mosquitoes, crickets and dragonflies are all insects.

Some insects are so small that you cannot see them well without a magnifier. Some are big. A giant stick insect can be longer than your hand.

Not every small animal is an insect. A **spider** has eight legs and two body parts, so it is not one. A **centipede** has many more than six legs. A **woodlouse** has fourteen legs. They are all relatives of insects, but they are not insects themselves.

Insects have lived on Earth for a very long time. They were here long before people, and they were here long before flowers. Their secret is simple: they are small, they eat a lot, and they have many babies.
examples: It has six legs, so it is an insect.
A spider has eight legs, so it is not an insect.
I found an ant on the kitchen floor.
sections.heading: What an insect is, and how to spot one

sections.body:
Look at any insect closely and the same plan appears every time.

The **head** comes first. It holds the eyes and the antennae. The antennae are the feelers that smell and hear. On the head there are also the mouth parts, which differ from insect to insect. A butterfly has a drinking tube. A beetle has strong jaws. A mosquito has a sharp needle.

The **thorax** is the middle part. All six legs attach here, and so do the wings, if the insect has them. The thorax is the engine room. It moves the legs and beats the wings.

The **abdomen** comes last. It is the soft, round back part. Inside it are the stomach and the organs that make eggs. You can often see the breathing holes along its sides. A wasp's abdomen is striped. A bee's abdomen shrinks into a sharp sting.

The body is covered by a hard shell called an **exoskeleton**. It protects the insect like a suit of armour. But it cannot stretch, so an insect must shed it to grow. A young insect sheds its skin several times before it is fully grown.

Insects also breathe in an unusual way. They do not have lungs. Air goes in through little holes along the body, straight into the tissues.
examples: The head has the eyes and the antennae.
All six legs grow out of the thorax.
The wasp's stripes are on its abdomen.
sections.heading: The three parts of an insect's body

sections.body:
These are the words that will let you talk about insects like a naturalist.

An **insect** is an animal with six legs and a body of three parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

Antennae are the pair of feelers on the head. Many insects use them to smell their way to food or to a mate.

The **exoskeleton** is the hard outer shell. It holds the insect together and keeps it safe, but it cannot grow.

The **thorax** is the middle body part. It carries all six legs and, in flying insects, the wings.

The **abdomen** is the back body part. It holds the gut and the organs that make eggs.

Metamorphosis is the big change of shape. A caterpillar becoming a butterfly is metamorphosis. Many insects go through it, and most do it in four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
sections.heading: The words about insects, one by one

terms.example: An ant is an insect because it has six legs.
terms.gloss: An animal with six legs and a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

terms.example: The beetle waves its antennae in the air.
terms.gloss: The two feelers on an insect's head. They help it smell and find its way.

terms.example: The empty shell of the cicada is left on the tree bark.
terms.gloss: The hard outer shell of an insect. It protects the body but cannot stretch, so the insect must shed it to grow.

terms.example: All six legs are attached to the thorax.
terms.gloss: The middle part of an insect's body. All six legs and the wings grow from it.

terms.example: The wasp's abdomen is yellow and black.
terms.gloss: The back part of an insect's body, where the stomach and the egg-making organs sit.

sections.body:
Insects are small, but the world would be very different without them.

Bees and butterflies carry pollen. Flowers make seeds only when pollen is moved from one flower to another. Bees do this job while they drink nectar. Many foods we eat depend on it, including apples, mangoes and rice.

Ants clean the ground. Ants carry dead insects and old food away. Without them, the ground would be much dirtier.

Ladybirds eat plant pests. A single ladybird may eat dozens of aphids, the tiny insects that eat leaves. Farmers and gardeners like ladybirds very much.

Bees make honey. A honey bee collects nectar and turns it into honey and into wax for the hive.

Insects feed other animals. Birds, frogs, fish, lizards and even some mammals eat insects. A bird raising three chicks may eat hundreds of insects in a day.

Insects clean up dead things. Some beetles and flies live on what is dead, and they return the goodness to the soil.

Insects were here first. The oldest known insect fossils are more than 400 million years old. Long before people existed, insects were eating plants and pollinating the first flowers.
examples: The bee carries pollen from flower to flower.
Ladybirds eat the aphids on the beans.
A swallow eats a lot of insects every day.
sections.heading: What insects do for us

sections.body:
Insects let you come very close. You do not need to catch them to learn about them.

Watch where insects go. Sit quietly near a flower and see who comes. Ants often have a path they use, and you can follow it with your eyes only.

Look at them in a clear box with a few leaves. Put the box in the shade and watch for a while. Then let the insect go, in the place where you found it.

Take a photo instead of catching them. A photo of a cicada on a tree can be better than a cicada in a jar.

Leave them their space. If you lift a stone to look underneath, put the stone back the way it was. Many small animals live under that stone and depend on it staying cool and dark.

And do not use bug spray near insects you are watching. It works on them very well, and that is the problem.
examples: I sit still and wait for the ants to come back.
I took a photo instead of catching it.
I put the stone back exactly where it was.
sections.heading: How to look at insects without hurting them
steps: Sit quietly near a flower and watch who comes.
Look in a clear box with a few leaves.
Take a photo rather than catching the insect.
Put stones and leaves back the way you found them.
Let the insect go where you found it.
Keep bug spray away from the place you watch.

sections.body:
Most insects are harmless. A few are not, and it is good to know which ones.

Stinging insects include bees, wasps and hornets. They sting when they are scared or when you grab them. A bee usually stings only once and then dies, because its sting stays behind with the venom.

Biting insects include mosquitoes, fleas and some flies. They want blood, because it helps them make eggs.

Sticky insects like aphids and scale insects suck plant sap. They do not bite you, but they weaken the plant.

Caterpillars can have itchy hairs. Some are also colourful on purpose, because bright colours warn animals to stay away.

If a bee flies near you, do not wave your arms. Walk away slowly. If you are stung, tell an adult, and clean the place with cool water.

And wash your hands after you are done playing outside. It keeps you and everybody else well.
examples: I walk away slowly when a bee comes close.
The caterpillar has bright colours, so I leave it alone.
I wash my hands after playing outside.
sections.heading: Insects that sting, and insects that bite

item.summary: Insects are small, but they are everywhere and they do enormous work. After reading this, you can spot an insect by its three body parts and six legs, learn what insects do for us, and watch them closely without hurting them.
item.title: The Wonderful World of Insects
